strengths: Soundness/significance: The empirical study is unusually broad, covering 8/14/20-task vision merging with two CLIP scales, NYUv2 dense prediction, GLUE, and corrupted images. SyMerge reports consistently strong results, often close to the individual experts, with means and standard deviations over five runs for the proposed method.

The component ablation provides useful evidence that adapting the task-specific layer and the merging coefficients is complementary: on 20 vision tasks, joint adaptation reaches 88.6 versus 81.6 and 75.0 for the respective single-component variants.

The transfer experiment is informative: SyMerge-adapted classifiers improve both Task Arithmetic and AdaMerging encoders, including cross-task evaluation. This supports the practically useful functional-alignment interpretation better than performance averages alone.

Originality/presentation: Jointly adapting one task-specific layer and layer-wise merging coefficients using expert-generated pseudo-labels is a simple, reasonably original combination. The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and supplies extensive per-task results, hyperparameters, convergence studies, and relevant ablations.
The limitations section honestly identifies dependence on expert quality. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the use of standard public benchmarks and models.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 1 is not proved. Equations (2) and (3) establish only that the synergistic case has a tighter convex upper bound; they do not establish that its actual expected loss is below that of the disentangled case. The unquantified approximation in cross-task linearity further prevents the claimed guarantee. Statements that the analysis “proves” superior merging should therefore be removed or substantially weakened.

The central claim of achieving task synergy is not convincingly demonstrated. In every main benchmark aggregate, SyMerge remains below the individual experts (for example, 90.1 versus 90.5 on eight-task ViT-B/32 and 83.9 versus 85.6 on GLUE). Most evidence instead shows effective transductive distillation from each task's expert into a shared encoder and adapted task head, which is valuable but does not establish that tasks mutually improve one another.

The pilot correlation does not establish the claimed predictive or causal relationship. Cross-task and merge accuracy share the same target task and are both confounded by target-task difficulty; the paper does not specify the precise observational units, control for task identity, report robustness across architectures, or test whether the relationship predicts unseen task pairs.

Evaluation fairness and practicality need stronger treatment. SyMerge requires running all individual experts on the unlabeled test set, whereas several baselines use substantially weaker signals. A direct multi-task knowledge-distillation baseline with the same expert predictions and compute budget is missing. Moreover, the appendix says sequential updates improve AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6, yet Table 1 reports 80.1, leaving unclear whether competitors received the stated improved protocol.

The method is transductive: it repeatedly optimizes for up to 1,000 iterations on the same test inputs later used for evaluation. This assumption is not clearly foregrounded, and there is no held-out or online adaptation experiment showing generalization to unseen post-adaptation samples. Runtime, expert-inference cost, memory/storage requirements, and parameter overhead from task-specific layer copies are also not reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter details. Code is only promised after publication; the new 14/20-task checkpoints, preprocessing, splits, seeds, exact pseudo-label construction, and task-specific losses are not fully specified. In particular, the treatment of regression tasks such as STS-B and dense depth/normal prediction remains ambiguous.

Presentation contains consequential overclaims, including calling individual models an upper bound, describing correlation as a reliable predictor, and interpreting a lower discrepancy count as improved generalization. The loss-correlation analysis also lacks a precise definition of the samples over which Spearman correlation is computed and does not establish alignment of optimization gradients.

The limitations discussion is too narrow: it mentions teacher quality but omits the flawed theoretical guarantee, test-set adaptation assumption, requirement to retain/run every expert, computational cost, and the limited evidence that the method produces genuine cross-task synergy. These issues prevent the current empirical gains from fully supporting the paper's stated contribution.

strengths: The empirical scope is broad: Table 1 evaluates 8-, 14-, and 20-task vision merging with two ViT scales, while Tables 2 and 3 extend the study to dense prediction and GLUE. SyMerge obtains strong results across these settings, often approaching the individual-model reference.

The component ablation in Table 5 supports the practical claim that jointly adapting merging coefficients and a task-specific layer performs better than adapting either component alone, especially as the number of vision tasks grows.

The paper includes useful diagnostic experiments, including per-layer adaptation (Figure 5 and Table B), loss comparisons, convergence curves, corruption results, and transfer of adapted classifiers to Task Arithmetic and AdaMerging encoders (Table 4).

The method is conceptually simple and clearly motivated. Reusing expert predictions as supervision also makes the objective applicable beyond classification, as illustrated by the dense-prediction experiments.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually well presented. It discloses test-time use of unlabeled data, reports five-run variation for SyMerge, provides substantial hyperparameter detail, and identifies dependence on expert quality as a limitation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. Proposition 1 only derives a tighter convex upper bound under an assumed synergistic effect. If L_B <= B_B and L_A <= B_A with B_B < B_A, it does not follow that L_B < L_A. Thus the proof cannot conclude that the synergistic merged model has lower actual expected loss than the disentangled case. Cross-task linearity is also approximate, but no approximation error is included. This is a major soundness problem because the paper presents the proposition as theoretical justification for its main thesis.

The experiments do not convincingly demonstrate the claimed cross-task 'synergy.' The main results show recovery toward the independently fine-tuned experts, while the method is explicitly trained to reproduce each task's own expert predictions on the evaluation inputs. The reported cross-task correlations and classifier-transfer results establish compatibility or alignment, not that knowledge from one task causally improves another. Performance generally remaining below the individual-model reference further weakens the claim that tasks actively enhance one another.

The evaluation is transductive: SyMerge optimizes on the unlabeled test examples and then reports performance on those same examples using labels from the corresponding expert. This may be legitimate test-time adaptation, but it makes the near-expert results substantially less surprising and leaves unanswered whether the adapted model generalizes to fresh samples. A held-out target split, streaming evaluation, or adaptation-then-evaluation protocol is needed.

The comparison is not information- or resource-matched. SyMerge must retain and run every fine-tuned expert to generate supervision, whereas entropy-based competitors do not receive expert predictions. The paper calls the approach lightweight and an efficient merging solution but reports no adaptation time, teacher-inference cost, peak memory, or comparison under equal access to experts. This omission is especially important for 20 tasks and ViT-L/14.

Baseline handling is insufficiently clear. Appendix A reports that a sequential update raises AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6, yet Table 1 uses 80.1, even while stating that experimental settings are identically applied to competing adaptive methods. Only SyMerge receives multi-run uncertainty, so the statistical reliability of claimed margins against reimplemented baselines cannot be assessed.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. Code is promised only after publication, the pseudo-label construction is not specified precisely enough to distinguish hard labels from soft targets, and several dataset/split, preprocessing, baseline-tuning, and computational-cost details are absent. Reported standard deviations cover only the proposed method.

The limitations discussion is too narrow. It acknowledges teacher quality but omits the same-test-set adaptation assumption, the need to store and execute all experts during adaptation, sensitivity to deployment batch availability or changing distributions, and the possibility that expert errors are directly propagated. These limitations materially constrain the claimed practical significance.

Overall, the method has promising empirical performance and a useful distillation-style adaptation recipe, but the invalid theoretical conclusion, lack of evidence for the defining synergy claim, and insufficiently controlled transductive comparison prevent acceptance in its present form.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical results are broad and strong. SyMerge consistently outperforms the reported merging baselines across 8/14/20-task vision settings and two CLIP scales (Table 1), while also extending successfully to NYUv2 dense prediction (Table 2) and eight GLUE tasks (Table 3).

The ablations are unusually useful: Table 5 separates coefficient and layer adaptation; Figure 5/Table B examine which and how many layers to adapt; Table 4 tests transfer to other merged encoders; and the appendix studies objectives, initialization, convergence, corruption robustness, and per-task performance.

Significance: Recovering performance close to independently fine-tuned experts—particularly as the number of tasks grows—is practically valuable. The method also avoids adding inference-time routing modules and applies beyond classification.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithmic intuition, experimental organization, and tables are generally clear. Reporting per-task results and five-run mean/standard deviation for SyMerge makes failure modes easier to inspect.

Originality: Jointly adapting merging coefficients and one task-specific layer through expert-guided self-labeling is a simple but useful combination. The emphasis on cross-task functional compatibility offers an interesting perspective on model merging.

Reproducibility and ethics: The appendix specifies optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, iteration counts, coefficient initialization, filtering, hardware, and checkpoints. The experiments use established public benchmarks, present no evident material ethical risk, and disclose limited LLM-assisted proofreading.
weaknesses: The central “synergy” interpretation is not convincingly established. SyMerge remains below the individual experts on average in every principal setting—for example, 90.1 versus 90.5 on eight-task ViT-B/32 and 83.9 versus 85.6 on GLUE. Distilling each task expert into a shared encoder with task-specific heads demonstrates effective preservation/alignment, but does not show that tasks mutually improve one another. No controlled leave-one-task-out experiment tests whether adding task i improves task j.

Proposition 1 is logically insufficient. It shows that the synergistic assumption produces a tighter Jensen upper bound than the non-interference assumption, but a lower upper bound does not imply that the actual merged-model loss is lower. Moreover, cross-task linearity is only approximate and is not empirically verified here. Thus the claimed guarantee and statement that the proof establishes a “superior model” are overstated.

The method adapts on the same unlabeled test samples used for reporting performance. This transductive protocol can be legitimate, but the manuscript does not clearly specify evaluation timing, whether samples are revisited, or performance on held-out data after adaptation. With 500–1,000 updates, this distinction matters for interpreting generalization and deployment.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently transparent. Appendix A reports that sequential updates improve AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6, yet Table 1 retains 80.1; it is unclear whether every adaptive baseline receives the proposed sequential schedule, confidence filtering, equal optimization effort, and tuning. Only SyMerge receives five-run error bars, preventing statistical comparison against the strongest baselines.

Claims of being “lightweight” and efficient lack measurements of training time, memory, expert-inference cost, and added task-specific parameters. Test-time training requires retaining and querying all expert models for pseudo-labels, while choosing an internal task-specific layer entails one copy per task; these costs should be compared with Surgery, ProbSurgery, and WEMoE.

Several implementation details remain underspecified, including the complete fine-tuning recipes for the new 14/20-task checkpoints, precise losses and pseudo-label construction for regression/dense tasks, dataset sampling or recycling during adaptation, and seed selection. Code is only promised after publication, so exact reproduction is not currently possible.

The limitations discussion acknowledges dependence on expert quality but omits more consequential limitations: transductive access to target test data, storage/inference requirements for all experts, possible confirmation of expert errors, fairness of adaptive comparisons, and the absence of demonstrated synergy beyond individual experts. These issues reduce confidence in the paper’s strongest claims, although the empirical method itself remains promising.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical results are extensive and consistently strong. SyMerge approaches individual-expert performance across 8/14/20 vision tasks and substantially outperforms adaptive-merging baselines on vision, NYUv2 dense prediction, RoBERTa GLUE, and FLAN-T5.

Soundness: The component ablations are informative: jointly adapting coefficients and one task-specific layer clearly outperforms either component alone, and evaluating the learned encoder with the original heads provides evidence that improvements are not solely due to head adaptation.

Significance: Expert-guided adaptation is simple and potentially useful in practice. The method uses relatively few trainable parameters, and the manuscript reports memory, runtime, data-scarcity, corruption, unreliable-expert, and backdoor stress tests.

Originality: Jointly optimizing merging coefficients and a single task-specific layer under expert pseudo-label supervision is a meaningful combination, especially its extension beyond classification to regression, dense prediction, and generation.
Presentation: The paper is generally clear and supplies substantial appendices, per-task results, hyperparameters, convergence studies, and five-run uncertainty estimates for the proposed method.

Limitations and ethics: The authors appropriately acknowledge dependence on expert quality, target-input access, privacy constraints, and possible propagation of expert bias. The corrupted- and backdoored-expert experiments are useful rather than grounds for penalizing the work.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 3.1 is not established by its proof. Jensen's inequality gives upper bounds in the non-interference and synergy cases, and one bound is tighter, but comparing upper bounds does not prove that the actual merged-model loss is lower. The use of approximate cross-task linearity further prevents the stated strict conclusion. This is important because the proposition is presented as theoretical support for the central claim.

Soundness: The evidence does not convincingly establish the claimed task synergy. The optimization teaches each task from its own expert, rather than supplying knowledge from other tasks, and the final averages generally remain below the individual experts. Cross-task correlation, supervised head retraining, and sample-level prediction discrepancies show compatibility or knowledge preservation, but do not demonstrate that one task causally improves another.

Soundness/evaluation: The method adapts on unlabeled test inputs and evaluates on those same inputs. This transductive protocol may be conventional for some adaptive-merging baselines, but it does not support the manuscript's broader claims about generalization under distribution shift. A held-out adaptation/evaluation split and a strictly prequential online evaluation are needed; the reported online experiment appears to update on each sample before evaluating that same sample.

Evaluation fairness: The appendix says sequential updates improve AdaMerging from 80.1 to 81.6 and that baselines are evaluated under the standardized sequential setting, yet the main comparison reports AdaMerging at 80.1. This inconsistency obscures whether all adaptive baselines received the same improved protocol.

Significance: The method requires access to every expert during adaptation to generate pseudo-labels, or storage of cached predictions. Thus it reduces final inference cost but is less clearly a standalone merging procedure than the framing suggests, and its adaptation-time storage and expert-inference requirements should be compared more explicitly with competing approaches.

Originality: Once the synergy interpretation is set aside, the core technique is close to test-time distillation from the original experts combined with AdaMerging-style coefficient optimization and head/layer fine-tuning. The manuscript does not isolate sufficiently what is conceptually new beyond this combination.

Evidence: The different-initialization result uses only one pair of tasks and pretrained checkpoints. Collapse of their weight average is not by itself a rigorous demonstration of disjoint loss basins, and one successful pair is insufficient for the broad claim that SyMerge can merge models from different initializations generally.

Reproducibility: The abstract's code statement ends at “available a” without a usable URL. Some reported tables also show apparent copy errors: in Table Q, the second block of Task Arithmetic values duplicates its first block exactly, and LiNeS exhibits the same duplication. Baseline uncertainty is not reported, while only SyMerge receives five-run error bars.

Presentation: The terminology “single task-specific layer” can be misleading because the appendix explains that selecting an internal layer creates a separate copy for every task. The resulting architecture, parameter accounting, and distinction from adapter-based multi-task models should be stated more directly in the main text.

Ethics: The limitations discussion is reasonable, but the generic impact statement understates concrete risks already exposed by the paper's own experiments, particularly propagation of backdoors, bias, or systematic expert errors through pseudo-label supervision.

The empirical scope is broad: the paper evaluates two CLIP scales on up to 20 vision tasks, RoBERTa and FLAN-T5 on GLUE, and ResNet-50 on three NYUv2 dense-prediction tasks. The reported average results are consistently strong relative to the included merging baselines—for example, 88.6 versus 86.6 for the strongest listed baseline on the 20-task ViT-B/32 setting.

The paper includes useful component ablations and diagnostics, including coefficient-only versus layer-only training, adaptation of different layers, limited-data and online settings, corrupted or backdoored experts, learning-rate sensitivity, and computational cost. The result that a SyMerge encoder retains an 82.4 average with the original heads, versus 69.1 for Task Arithmetic, is particularly helpful evidence that the result is not entirely classifier memorization.

Efficiency is considered explicitly. The method uses 0.39M trainable parameters for ViT-B/32, has peak adaptation memory close to AdaMerging, and can reduce per-step runtime through cached expert predictions.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on expert quality and the need for target inputs; the paper also tests corrupted and backdoored experts rather than merely mentioning these concerns.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is invalid as stated. Proposition 3.1 compares two Jensen upper bounds and observes that one upper bound is smaller; this does not imply that the actual merged-model loss is smaller than in the weight-disentangled case. Moreover, cross-task linearity is only approximate, while the proof treats it as equality. Thus the conclusion that the proposition “proves” a superior merged model is unsupported.

The experiments do not establish the paper's central claim of synergy. Synergy is defined as one task actively improving another, yet SyMerge remains below the individual-expert average in essentially every main aggregate result (e.g., 90.1 versus 90.5 on 8-task ViT-B/32 and 83.9 versus 85.6 on RoBERTa). Figure 5 reports that negative-transfer cases still outnumber positive-transfer cases; SyMerge merely has the smallest positive discrepancy. This supports interference reduction or expert imitation, not positive transfer beyond the experts.

The pilot evidence does not bridge this gap. Its classifiers are retrained with ground-truth training labels, whereas SyMerge is trained using expert pseudo-labels, and the method does not directly optimize the proposed cross-task metric. The reported correlation of 0.863 is computed over target-task averages and can be strongly confounded by task difficulty: targets that are easier under foreign encoders may also be easier after merging. No controlled or pair-level analysis establishes a causal connection.

The method is close to multi-teacher self-distillation layered on AdaMerging/Representation Surgery, but the evaluation lacks a strong matched distillation baseline—for example, training the same task-specific layer or an equally sized student on expert outputs while keeping a conventional merged encoder, and allowing comparable encoder adaptation. Coefficient-only and layer-only ablations do not isolate whether the claimed novelty matters relative to ordinary expert distillation. The large advantage over entropy minimization is also unsurprising because SyMerge receives substantially richer supervision from task experts.

The different-initialization result is substantially overclaimed. It uses only one EuroSAT/DTD pair, defines task vectors specially around their weight average, and provides no repetitions, alternative model pairs, or analysis of why one task-specific layer recovers such large accuracy despite the asserted loss barrier. It cannot support the general claim that SyMerge merges models from different initializations, especially when this setting explicitly violates the assumption used by the paper's theory.

Statistical support is uneven. Only SyMerge is reported with variation over five runs in the main tables, while baseline results are point estimates. Some baselines are reimplemented with a sequential-update procedure that changes their performance, and initialization is changed from 0.3 to 0.1 for the larger task collections because 0.3 performs poorly. Without matched repeated trials and a transparent validation protocol, small margins cannot be interpreted confidently.

The evaluation is transductive: the method adapts on unlabeled test inputs and then evaluates on those inputs using predictions from the original experts. This is permissible as test-time adaptation but narrows the claimed applicability and makes comparisons to training-free merging methods intrinsically unequal. The paper should more sharply distinguish model merging from post-hoc distillation and evaluate held-out generalization after adaptation.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the complexity of the study. The abstract's code reference is an unresolved “a” rather than a usable repository, and there is no complete algorithm or pseudocode. Important details remain ambiguous, including coefficient constraints, seed selection, precise train/test adaptation protocol, preprocessing and checkpoint construction for the added vision tasks, and task-specific losses and layer definitions for dense prediction and NLP.

The ethics discussion is perfunctory. The impact statement says no consequences require discussion even though the method propagates predictions from potentially biased or compromised experts and requires access to target inputs. The backdoor experiment still reports a 75.6% off-task attack success rate for SyMerge, which is lower than the baselines but remains a serious vulnerability that should not be framed as robustness without stronger qualification.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical results are broad and consistently strong. SyMerge substantially outperforms adaptive and training-free baselines across 8/14/20-task vision merging, NYUv2 dense prediction, RoBERTa and FLAN-T5 GLUE settings; the gains generally persist for two CLIP scales.

The evaluation includes valuable diagnostics beyond aggregate accuracy: component ablations, per-task results, layer-choice studies, convergence and learning-rate analyses, limited-data and online settings, corrupted distributions, unreliable/backdoored experts, and computational cost. Jointly adapting coefficients and one task-specific layer is convincingly better than adapting either alone, especially at 20 tasks (88.6 versus 81.6 and 75.0).

Significance: The method is practical within its stated test-time setting. It approaches individual-expert performance while retaining a shared encoder, adds only 0.39M trainable parameters for ViT-B/32, and extends beyond classification to dense prediction and regression-like objectives.

Originality: Joint coefficient optimization and single-layer, expert-guided adaptation is a simple but useful combination. The transferable-head and fixed-original-head experiments provide evidence that optimization improves the shared encoder rather than merely memorizing through the adapted classifier.

Presentation and reproducibility are generally good: the manuscript is readable, supplies optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, iteration, initialization, and sequential-update details, and reports five-run uncertainty for SyMerge's main results. Limitations concerning expert quality, privacy, and latency are acknowledged, and the backdoor experiments improve the ethical treatment of model-supply-chain risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical proposition is not established. Jensen's inequality only gives a tighter upper bound under the assumed synergistic condition; comparing two upper bounds does not prove that the realized merged-model loss is lower than under weight disentanglement. Moreover, cross-task linearity is approximate, while the proposition and proof do not quantify approximation error. Cosine similarities of outputs are insufficient to bound the relevant loss error.

The paper's framing overstates demonstrated 'synergy.' Most aggregate SyMerge results remain below the individual-expert reference (for example, 90.1 versus 90.5 on 8-task ViT-B/32), so the evidence mainly establishes recovery of expert behavior through self-distillation and reduced interference. Sample-level positive transfers and a few per-task improvements do not by themselves show that tasks mutually improve one another overall.

Evaluation is transductive: expert pseudo-labels are produced on the target test inputs, optimization is performed on those inputs, and performance is then measured on the same test set. This is a legitimate test-time-adaptation protocol but does not support the manuscript's broader claims of generalization under distribution shift. A held-out target split or adapt-then-evaluate protocol is needed; the online experiment is especially optimistic because each sample is updated on before being evaluated.

The method requires retaining and querying every expert during adaptation, and uses one task-specific copy of the selected layer per task. Consequently, the full storage/inference burden scales with the number of experts even though the reported trainable-parameter and peak-GPU-memory numbers are small. Comparisons against training-free methods should more clearly separate this stronger data-and-expert-access setting.

There are reporting and reproducibility concerns. Table Q's ViT-L/14 20-task Task Arithmetic and LiNeS results for the final ten tasks exactly duplicate their respective first-ten-task values, and the reported averages therefore appear unreliable. Baseline uncertainty is omitted, the claimed code link is not usable in the manuscript, and some implementation choices—such as task ordering and checkpoint/model selection—are not specified precisely enough for exact reproduction.

The novelty is moderate rather than exceptional: expert-guided pseudo-labeling is standard distillation, and the main technical contribution is its combination with adaptive merging and one trainable task-specific layer. The correlation between cross-task and merge performance is observational and does not establish the claimed causal mechanism.
